The bond market was going bonkers, and relatively untested Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had to do something . So Wednesday morning, he announced the U.S. government would buy up more bonds. This bond-market Band-Aid calmed things down a bit, but it’s not a long-term solution.

   Bessent is a curious character in Trump 2.0. The tough talk bravado doesn’t come as naturally to him as it does to some other members of the cabinet, though that doesn’t stop him from trying at cabinet meetings or in television appearances.

   The truth of the 2026 economy isn’t an easy one to put on a bumper sticker. Yes, the stock market is near record highs and the unemployment rate is relatively low. But hiring has slowed. The bond market is worrisome, and budget deficits are very stretched.

   Meanwhile, Bessent has pledged to help two Trump-friendly governments in Argentina and Japan, putting a bit more political spin on fiscal policy than we normally see.

   I’ve covered eight Treasury secretaries. There’s always an awkward political element to these jobs that none of them ever quite master. John Snow traveled heavily to Ohio in 2004 to promote the economic agenda (it just so happened George W. Bush wanted badly to win Ohio, and Snow was from there). Hank Paulson got down on a knee at one point during the financial crisis to coax Democrats to help with a bailout. I went with Jack Lew to China in 2013 to meet the country’s new leader, Xi Jinping. I went with Steven Mnuchin to Baden-Baden, Germany.

   Last week, when the bond market was fritzing, Bessent was in Iowa with two Republicans running in tight election races (it felt like half of Trump’s cabinet has visited Iowa in the past week).

   These Treasury jobs, at the end of the day, are to keep financial markets moving smoothly and prevent fiascos. They can get dragged into politics, but that’s not their job. They are third in line to the presidency for a reason. Getting the balance right is easier said than done.

   If Bessent blows it, and the bond market can’t be sweet-talked, the political races in Iowa will be the least of his problems.

Gross U.S. debt has surpassed $40 trillion for the first time, a new milestone in the country’s struggle to control its finances. The country’s “total public debt outstanding” officially hit $40.047 trillion on Tuesday, the Treasury Department reported. The U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio is widely expected to keep rising—reaching 120% in 10 years and 175% in 30 years, the Congressional Budget Office said.

   The military’s drone unit is being phased out as part of a “basic to basics” approach. A much touted drone assault battalion set up by the Army is being eliminated by the four-star general aligned with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It is part of a “back-to-basics” approach ordered up by Gen. Christopher LaNeve. But the decision is drawing criticism from military experts who say it will hamper the Army’s ability to develop proficiency in drone tactics.

Four Senate Democrats asked the Federal Reserve chairman to publicly disclose his conversations with the president, after The Wall Street Journal reported this month that the two have spoken repeatedly since he became Fed chairman, and Warsh’s appointment calendars showed no such calls. The lawmakers said undisclosed contacts risk creating “a perception that the White House is shaping monetary policy.”

   Trump threatens Iran with “Economic D-Day.” The president vowed to unleash a major economic campaign against Iran and any entity that does business with the regime as frustrations mount over lack of progress on reopening the Strait of Hormuz or reaching a deal to end the nearly six-month war.

   • The U.S. is likely to lower tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum and automobiles as part of a trade framework.

   • The Federal Trade Commission warns companies they must disclose when they use a shopper’s personal data to calculate how much they charge for a good or service.

   • The U.S. military is returning to the Philippines decades after it left at the end of the Cold War, as the nation becomes pivotal to U.S. strategy against China.

Scott Bessent and the Art of the Treasury Tightrope
 
Plus, U.S. debt reaches $40 trillion, and the Army cuts a much-heralded drone unit as it goes ‘back to basics’
 
 
GRAEME SLOAN/PRESS POOL
 

Good morning. The bond market was going bonkers, and relatively untested Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had to do something. So Wednesday morning, he announced the U.S. government would buy up more bonds. This bond-market Band-Aid calmed things down a bit, but it’s not a long-term solution.

 

Bessent is a curious character in Trump 2.0. The tough talk bravado doesn’t come as naturally to him as it does to some other members of the cabinet, though that doesn’t stop him from trying at cabinet meetings or in television appearances.

 

The truth of the 2026 economy isn’t an easy one to put on a bumper sticker. Yes, the stock market is near record highs and the unemployment rate is relatively low. But hiring has slowed. The bond market is worrisome, and budget deficits are very stretched.

 

Meanwhile, Bessent has pledged to help two Trump-friendly governments in Argentina and Japan, putting a bit more political spin on fiscal policy than we normally see.

 

I’ve covered eight Treasury secretaries. There’s always an awkward political element to these jobs that none of them ever quite master. John Snow traveled heavily to Ohio in 2004 to promote the economic agenda (it just so happened George W. Bush wanted badly to win Ohio, and Snow was from there). Hank Paulson got down on a knee at one point during the financial crisis to coax Democrats to help with a bailout. I went with Jack Lew to China in 2013 to meet the country’s new leader, Xi Jinping. I went with Steven Mnuchin to Baden-Baden, Germany.

 

Last week, when the bond market was fritzing, Bessent was in Iowa with two Republicans running in tight election races (it felt like half of Trump’s cabinet has visited Iowa in the past week).

 

These Treasury jobs, at the end of the day, are to keep financial markets moving smoothly and prevent fiascos. They can get dragged into politics, but that’s not their job. They are third in line to the presidency for a reason. Getting the balance right is easier said than done.

 

If Bessent blows it, and the bond market can’t be sweet-talked, the political races in Iowa will be the least of his problems.

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Angie Nixon: The Democratic Socialist harnessed complaints about affordability to come out of nowhere and claim her party’s Senate nomination in Florida.

 

Trump’s Ballroom: The Supreme Court will soon decide whether to allow the president to continue building the $400 million project.

 

Trump’s Thursday: The president is scheduled to participate in a pretaped radio interview at 9 a.m. ET, hold a policy meeting at 11 a.m., participate in signing time at 2 p.m. and take part in a Fostering the Future announcement at 4 p.m.

What I’m Following

 

U.S. debt reaches $40 trillion—how did we get here? Gross U.S. debt has surpassed $40 trillion for the first time, a new milestone in the country’s struggle to control its finances. The country’s “total public debt outstanding” officially hit $40.047 trillion on Tuesday, the Treasury Department reported. The U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio is widely expected to keep rising—reaching 120% in 10 years and 175% in 30 years, the Congressional Budget Office said.

 

The military’s drone unit is being phased out as part of a “basic to basics” approach. A much touted drone assault battalion set up by the Army is being eliminated by the four-star general aligned with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It is part of a “back-to-basics” approach ordered up by Gen. Christopher LaNeve. But the decision is drawing criticism from military experts who say it will hamper the Army’s ability to develop proficiency in drone tactics.

 

Democrats want more details of Kevin Warsh’s calls with Trump. Four Senate Democrats asked the Federal Reserve chairman to publicly disclose his conversations with the president, after The Wall Street Journal reported this month that the two have spoken repeatedly since he became Fed chairman, and Warsh’s appointment calendars showed no such calls. The lawmakers said undisclosed contacts risk creating “a perception that the White House is shaping monetary policy.”

 

Trump threatens Iran with “Economic D-Day.” The president vowed to unleash a major economic campaign against Iran and any entity that does business with the regime as frustrations mount over lack of progress on reopening the Strait of Hormuz or reaching a deal to end the nearly six-month war.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Trump’s plan to squeeze Iran’s economy will live or die in Dubai.

 

• Minutes from the Fed’s July meeting show more officials favored raising interest rates last month than the three who formally dissented.

 

• The U.S. is likely to lower tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum and automobiles as part of a trade framework.

 

• The Federal Trade Commission warns companies they must disclose when they use a shopper’s personal data to calculate how much they charge for a good or service.

 

• The U.S. military is returning to the Philippines decades after it left at the end of the Cold War, as the nation becomes pivotal to U.S. strategy against China.
